identity.title: Ascites signs: shifting dullness, flank dullness, fluid wave, bulging flanks

technique.how: Supine: inspect for bulging flanks, then percuss from the umbilicus laterally to map the level of flank dullness. Roll the patient 45-90 degrees toward you and re-percuss; dullness that migrates to the dependent side (tympany above) is shifting dullness. Fluid wave: assistant's ulnar edge on the midline, tap one flank and feel the impulse on the other.
technique.prerequisites: Patient able to lie supine and roll; bladder empty; wait a few seconds after rolling before re-percussing.
technique.contraindications: None absolute; avoid rolling if unstable spine or recent abdominal surgery.

interpretation.positive_finding: A fluid wave (LR+ 9.6) or shifting dullness (LR+ 5.76) substantially raises the probability of ascites; an examiner's overall impression 'suggestive of ascites' had LR+ 37.7-83.3.
interpretation.negative_finding: Absence of bulging flanks (LR- 0.12) argues strongly against ascites; absent flank dullness excluded ascites with >90% accuracy in Cattau 1982. Absent shifting dullness alone is less reassuring.
interpretation.pitfalls: Small-volume (<1 L) ascites is missed; obesity produces false-positive flank dullness and false-negative fluid waves; a fluid wave needs a large volume. In low-prevalence groups (normal PT) positive signs were usually false positives (Cummings 1985).
interpretation.changes_what: Positive: proceed to diagnostic paracentesis (rule out SBP if febrile/AMS/AKI). Negative with low pretest odds: ascites unlikely; if still suspected, bedside ultrasound.

sources.citation: Williams JW Jr, Simel DL. The rational clinical examination. Does this patient have ascites? How to divine fluid in the abdomen. JAMA. 1992;267(19):2645-2648.
Simel DL, Halvorsen RA Jr, Feussner JR. Quantitating bedside diagnosis: clinical evaluation of ascites. J Gen Intern Med. 1988;3(5):423-428.
Cattau EL Jr, Benjamin SB, Knuff TE, Castell DO. The accuracy of the physical examination in the diagnosis of suspected ascites. JAMA. 1982;247(8):1164-1166.
Cummings S, Papadakis M, Melnick J, Gooding GA, Tierney LM Jr. The predictive value of physical examinations for ascites. West J Med. 1985;142(5):633-636.

safety_scope.do_not_use_when: Do not rely on exam alone to exclude small-volume ascites when SBP or hepatorenal syndrome is the question; use ultrasound.
safety_scope.escalation_warning: New or worsening ascites with fever, abdominal pain, encephalopathy or rising creatinine mandates paracentesis and SBP work-up the same day.
safety_scope.interobserver_note: Simel 1988 reported LRs per examiner as ranges (e.g. overall evaluation 37.7-83.3), indicating examiner-dependent performance; Cattau 1982 used three independent examiners with overall accuracy only 58%.

extraction_notes: The 1992 RCE (PMID 1573754) has no PubMed abstract and no PMC text, so its pooled table could not be viewed; it is cited as the anchoring review but no number is taken from it. Numbers come from the abstract of Simel 1988 (the RCE's core primary study): LR+ fluid wave 9.6, LR+ shifting dullness 5.76, LR- absent bulging flanks 0.12; no CIs, sensitivity or specificity are given in the abstract, so those fields are null. Cattau 1982 (21 patients, 6 with ascites) reports only ranges (sens 50-94%, spec 29-82%) and that absent flank dullness excludes ascites with >90% accuracy - not entered as a per-sign estimate. Cummings 1985 reports positive predictive values (shifting dullness 51%, fluid wave 73%; 96% for fluid wave when PT prolonged) and 2% ascites with normal PT and no shifting dullness - PPVs, not sens/spec, so not entered. Status partially_quantified.
